transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Start time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CTO - Opal), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng - Opal), Priya Reddy (Platform Eng - Opal)

Summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategies for Opal Analytics. Discussed cache keys, tenant isolation, hit-rate expectations, KV/prefix cache semantics for long context windows, batching/latency tradeoffs, quantization effects on cacheability, and private/VPC deployment constraints. Agreed next steps: share design doc, run private benchmark, follow-up meeting.

Topics: prefix caching, cache keys, multi-tenant safety, hit rates, KV cache, batching, quantization, VPC/on-prem deployment

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: all right everyone thanks for jumping on, um quick intros then we'll dive in. i'm avery, account lead at redwood.
[00:12] Maya: hi i'm maya, cto at opal. thanks for doing this deep dive.
[00:15] Liam: liam here, i'll be owning the benchmarks and infra side.
[00:18] Priya: priya, platform eng, primarily around VPC and network constraints.
[00:22] Devon: hey team, devon from redwood, i'll take the technical run and whiteboard the cache key options.
[00:28] Avery: our goal today is to go through prefix-caching approach, what we can guarantee in hosted vs dedicated vs private, and then figure out a safe multi-tenant strategy for your use-case, which i know has dynamic prompts and a mix of templated and free-form user input.
[00:42] Maya: yes our prompts are a lot of templated system messages + user queries, heavy personalization. we care about low tail latency for inference and also strict data isolation in private mode.
[00:52] Devon: cool. quick agenda: 1) recap how redwood's KV/prefix cache works in runtime, 2) cache key design patterns, 3) hit-rate sizing and instrumentation, 4) multi-tenant safety and tenant scoping, 5) batching and quantization interactions, 6) ops and on-prem considerations. sound good?
[01:06] Maya: perfect.
[01:08] --
[01:12] Devon: starting from the runtime: our engine keeps a per-worker KV cache of past key/values for transformer layers, keyed by a short fingerprint of the prefix (we often use xxhash64 or blake2b in the design doc). cache entries are the serialized KV tensors for a given model version and sequence position. when a request arrives, we try to match a prefix fingerprint and replay cached KVs so the model only computes from the cached point forward.
[01:39] Liam: is the cache per-model? per-worker? what's the eviction policy?
[01:44] Devon: good Q. it's per-model-version per-worker by default, with an LRU eviction and size based on tokens stored. we also support global shard-level caches for dedicated pools. eviction is token-count based, TTL optional.
[01:57] Priya: for on-prem private deployments, can the cache be persisted across restarts? we want warm starts.
[02:02] Devon: yes, we have optional persisted cache to NFS/S3 or local SSD for private. note: persisted cache means you need to be careful about model version compatibility and serialization format.
[02:12] Maya: how do you do prefix matching with noisy user inputs? our prompts often have small per-user tokens like timestamps or session IDs that break exact matches.
[02:20] Devon: this is the key design decision. we recommend a two-tier key: 1) canonicalized prefix fingerprint (strip stable volatile fields, apply deterministic template extraction), 2) a secondary fuzzy-match TTL for near matches. so you can get high hit rate for templated parts while falling back safely. in practice we add a hash of the model version + prefix-type + canonicalized content.
[02:45] Liam: canonicalization sounds heavy. do you provide helpers?
[02:47] Devon: yes, we ship a canonicalization library in the SDK—regex-based templates, token-level replacements, and a suggestion tool that scans sample prompts and proposes canonicalization rules.
[02:58] Maya: what about privacy—if some cached prefixes contain PII, and we're multi-tenant, how do you prevent leakage?
[03:05] Devon: we scope cache keys by tenant id and by deployment isolation. for hosted shared pools we recommend tenant-scoped keys (prefix + tenant hash). for Dedicated you get isolated GPU pools so cache is naturally segregated. for Private, obviously the cache is within your network. plus we support encryption-at-rest for persisted caches.
[03:23] Priya: okay but for co-located multi-tenant shared hardware is tenant hash sufficient? i'm worried about side-channels.
[03:30] Devon: tenant hash prevents accidental key collisions but does not eliminate microarchitectural side-channels; if you need hard tenant separation we recommend Dedicated or Private. additionally we provide ACLs and audit logs so any cache evictions or cache reads are tracked per-tenant.
[03:46] Liam: can we store only prefixes and never store full user content? like store only normalized embeddings or some masked KV that removes tokens marked as sensitive?
[03:56] Devon: you can. we have a 'sensitive mode' where we store masked KVs—the runtime zeros out positions marked by a mapping table before persisting. there's a tradeoff: more masking reduces cache hit fidelity and increases recomputation.
[04:10] Maya: let's talk hit rates—what should we expect for our templated system? we saw a 30% hit rate in your demo but that was a simple use-case.
[04:19] Devon: hit rates vary a lot. for mostly templated system messages + short user prompts, we typically see 40-70% on prefix length 64-256 tokens. with your mix (templated initial context + personalization tokens) i'd estimate 35-55% with canonicalization. we'll need your sample traffic to model it more precisely.
[04:36] Liam: by hit rate do you mean exact KV reuse at the same layer positions? how do you measure partial hits?
[04:42] Devon: yes, we measure exact prefix fingerprint hits (full prefix match) and also partial hits where some initial layers' KVs are reused and then we compute the rest. metrics emitted: prefix_hits, partial_prefix_hits, hit_bytes_saved, tokens_reused.
[04:57] Priya: how do caching and batching interact? we need to preserve tail latency SLAs.
[05:02] Devon: caching reduces per-request compute, so it usually helps latency. but batching introduces queueing delay. our routing tries to make batching adaptive: low-latency requests are routed to a fast lane with small batches; cached requests can be aggregated more aggressively because compute is lighter. you can configure the batching policy per-route.
[05:21] Maya: are there risk of stale caches after a model rollback or prompt template change?
[05:26] Devon: yes. caches are tagged by model checksum and prompt-version tag. when you roll back a model or update templates we suggest incrementing the prefix-version tag which invalidates old entries. we also provide a cache-invalidation API to purge keys by tag.
[05:41] Liam: about quantization—if we run int8 or 4-bit kernels, does that change cache serialization and reuse?
[05:47] Devon: the KVs are numeric tensors dependent on kernel/quantization. we include quantization profile in the cache key (model version + quant profile). we also have a conversion layer: if a cached KV is stored in fp16 and the runtime uses int8, we can optionally dequantize/requantize but that costs CPU and may degrade quality. best practice: keep a quant-profile aligned between cache writers and readers.
[06:11] Priya: so for private on-prem we must standardize the quant profile in our deployment plan. who manages that?
[06:15] Devon: in Private deployments the customer controls the runtime config; Redwood's packaging includes recommended profiles and a small CLI to set quant config. we'll include a recommended profile file in the design doc.
[06:26] Maya: any specific guidance for long context windows? we sometimes have 8k windows with long system plus conversation history. does caching break down?
[06:33] Devon: longer contexts increase the KV storage size; eviction pressure goes up. we recommend hierarchical caching: store a small per-session prefix for the most recent context and a separate coarse-grained cache for stable system prefixes. also you can checkpoint KVs at major conversation turns to reduce recompute.
[06:48] Liam: curious, any influence of attention optimizations? we've heard about flash-attention and its interaction with KV layout.
[06:54] Devon: yep, kernel selection matters. our runtime chooses kernels based on seq-len distribution; cached KVs must match expected layout. we do some format normalization on cache persistence so it works across kernel variants, but crossing too-different kernels may require re-materialization.
[07:08] --
[07:12] Priya: network-wise, for VPC private mode, are we shipping cache traffic across the control plane or purely inside data plane?
[07:19] Devon: cache persistence sync (if enabled) goes over customer-configured storage (S3 or internal object store) inside your VPC. runtime traffic is peer-to-peer inside the cluster. control-plane metadata is minimal and can be disabled for Private.
[07:33] Maya: okay. for our compliance team, can you provide audit logs that show cache access per-tenant and timestamps?
[07:40] Devon: yes, we provide audit logs with cache hits/evictions annotated per-tenant and per-model. retention configurable. we'll include a sample log schema in the security addendum.
[07:51] Liam: what's the memory overhead per cached token roughly? we need to size nodes.
[07:56] Devon: approximate: for FP16 KVs, ~16 bytes per parameter per-token per-layer; for 8-bit quant profiles it's less but variable. an easier rule: for a 70B model with 40 layers, storing 1024 tokens of KVs per worker is on the order of tens of GB. the design doc has a sizing calc—we'll populate it with your model shape.
[08:17] Maya: let's discuss cache keys concretely. show us the candidate key formats.
[08:21] Devon: sure. candidate A (exact): hash(model_ver || prefix_raw). Candidate B (canonical): hash(model_ver || prefix_canonical || tenant_id). Candidate C (templated fingerprint + slot-hash): hash(model_ver || template_id || slot_signature || tenant_id). We also add quant_profile and runtime_tag.
[08:41] Priya: template_id and slot_signature—does the SDK extract these automatically?
[08:45] Devon: the SDK can auto-propose template ids based on clustering common prompts; slots are the variable tokens. you can accept or override proposals.
[08:54] Liam: what about key length and storage indexing? collision risk?
[08:57] Devon: we use 64 or 128-bit fingerprints; collision risk is negligible in practice but we include collision detection heuristics—if two different prefixes map to same fingerprint but differ at runtime we mark entry as suspect and recompute, also log for ops.
[09:13] Maya: performance testing—could we run a benchmark where you replay our traffic across hosted vs dedicated vs private and show latency distributions and hit-rate delta?
[09:22] Devon: yes that's the plan. we'll need your 7-day sample trace and model files. we'll run three configs: hosted shared pool with tenant-scoped keys, dedicated pool with shared cache inside pool, and private on-prem with persisted cache.
[09:35] Liam: what metrics will you collect?
[09:38] Devon: raw p50/p90/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, prefix_hits, partial_hits, cache_evictions, memory usage, and cost model (estimated $/1M tokens) for hosted.
[09:51] Priya: about eviction—can we pin certain prefixes to never evict? like legal disclaimers or system prompts?
[09:57] Devon: yes, pinning is supported; pinned entries are excluded from LRU and persisted. but pinning increases memory footprint so plan capacity accordingly.
[10:07] Maya: are there safety issues if a pinned prefix contains a bug in system prompt? we could keep bad content cached.
[10:13] Devon: good catch—pinning should be used carefully. we recommend test/approval flow before pinning and a canary period. you can also pin in a read-only cache snapshot separate from live patchable cache.
[10:26] --
[10:30] Liam: let's talk about instrumentation and dashboards. we want per-route dashboards.
[10:34] Devon: Redwood Console emits per-route metrics: hit-rate heatmaps, token-saved, and cluster-level memory. Alerts can be set for cache-thrashing, sudden drop in hit-rate (template drift), or high eviction rates.
[10:47] Maya: template drift detection—can you detect when minor prompt changes reduce hit rates and suggest canonicalization rules?
[10:54] Devon: yes, we have a drift detector that clusters failed prefix matches and surfaces common differences and proposed regex/template rules. it's not perfect but helps ops.
[11:03] Priya: what about partial reuse—can we reuse KVs for first N layers only and compute rest? how do you account for that in latency?
[11:11] Devon: partial reuse is supported; we measure layer_reuse_percentage and runtime uses it to skip early layers' compute. partial reuse still gives decent latency wins and is tracked separately in metrics.
[11:22] Maya: ok. operations question: if we run private on-prem with persistent cache to s3 gateway, how do we back up and restore cache state across upgrades?
[11:30] Devon: the persistence format is snapshot + incremental log. for upgrades we recommend snapshot export, validate compatibility via checksum tool, and then import. we'll run an upgrade checklist with you.
[11:42] Liam: security: what about encryption for cache in transit and at rest?
[11:46] Devon: TLS for transit, and AES-256 for at-rest with KMS/HSM integration for Private. for Hosted we manage keys but you can bring your own via KMS in Dedicated/Private.
[11:58] --
[12:02] Maya: are there known failure modes? like corrupt cache entries causing silent quality regression?
[12:08] Devon: yes possible. we include checksums and a 'safety_recompute' fallback: on suspicious outputs we can force recompute and mark the entry. additionally our quality monitors tie outputs to eval prompts and will alert on distribution drift.
[12:20] Liam: could caching amplify hallucinations if a bad prefix got cached?
[12:24] Devon: it could, which is why we have TTLs, controlled pinning, and quality guards. we recommend coupling caching with evaluation-based regression alerts so if a pinned prefix degrades quality you can invalidate it automatically.
[12:38] Priya: network egress concerns: if cache persistence hits external S3, egress could be large. do you support local object stores only?
[12:45] Devon: yes local object stores supported. for Private we run everything inside VPC and don't traverse the public internet. you can also disable persistence and accept warmer starts.
[12:58] --
[13:02] Avery: quick recap and proposed pilot: 1) Opal shares 7-day sample trace + model binary, 2) Redwood runs 24-hour replay on private config and returns hit-rate/latency/cost tradeoffs, 3) we deliver cache-key recommendations and SDK canonicalization suggestions, 4) follow-up meeting to review results.
[13:22] Maya: agreed. tentative go/no-go for pilot next week, will confirm after internal security triage.
[13:28] Liam: timeline is fine. i'll get the traffic dump in by friday 2025-12-05.
[13:33] Devon: we'll also include a sample helm values file for Private and a sample quant-profile.
[13:38] Priya: please include network diagram for persistence and control-plane interactions.
[13:42] Avery: action items noted. we'll send the design doc and security addendum after this call.
[13:49] Maya: thanks everyone.
[13:50] Avery: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
